findings.message: Option d is word-for-word identical to keyed option a (only prefixed with "Proceed as follows:"), so two options state the same correct action while only a is keyed; a learner cannot pick a single answer. Option d's "why" text and the explanation's mention of a private CA show the intended distractor text was lost.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace option d's text with the intended private-CA distractor, e.g. "Issue the certificate from AWS Private CA and select it as the distribution's custom SSL certificate.", keeping its existing "why" explanation.

findings.message: The explanation rebuts a local secondary index ("cannot be added after table creation and would share the hot key"), but no option offers an LSI — only a GSI (option f). The stray rebuttal can confuse learners matching the explanation to the options.
findings.suggestedFix: Drop the LSI clause, e.g. end with: "...and a global secondary index keyed on the same hot date leaves that single partition where it is, since index writes are distributed by the index's own partition key."

findings.message: The card's central API surface claims — the client class `AnthropicBedrockMantle` and the endpoint `https://bedrock-mantle.{region}.api.aws/anthropic/v1/messages` — differ from the long-standing `AnthropicBedrock` client and `bedrock-runtime.{region}.amazonaws.com` host, and cannot be confirmed; since the whole answer hinges on them they should be re-verified against current Anthropic/AWS documentation.
findings.suggestedFix: Confirm the exact class name and endpoint host/path against the current "Claude on Amazon Bedrock" documentation, and add a source.url/quote so learners (and future reviewers) can verify them.

findings.message: The stem scopes the question to "Opus 4.7 and later", but the answer never explains what that version boundary changes (the example model is claude-opus-5), so the qualifier in the stem is unexplained and the pricing note (global vs. regional 10% premium) answers nothing the stem asks.
findings.suggestedFix: Either state in the explanation why the new client/endpoint applies only from Opus 4.7 onward (and what earlier models use), or drop the parenthetical from the stem; likewise move the global/regional pricing sentence into the stem's scope or remove it.

findings.message: The stem appends "Hint: the correct option begins \"Put an Amazon CloudFront distribution in front of the Network ...\"", which literally identifies the keyed option (a) verbatim; a learner with no knowledge of WAF target resources can pick it from the cue alone.
findings.suggestedFix: Delete the entire "Hint: ..." sentence from the question stem so the stem ends at "...with the LEAST amount of change?"

findings.message: The stem's qualifier is "LOWEST cost", but neither the explanation nor any distractor "why" argues cost — all three rejections are based on operational overhead (patching, AMIs, fleet sizing), and on pure cost Fargate is not clearly lowest (an EC2 launch type or self-managed node fleet on Spot/Reserved capacity can be cheaper for the same workload). The keyed option wins on the criterion the stem states in prose (no time to build AMIs, patch OS, right-size fleets), not on the stated qualifier.
findings.suggestedFix: Change the qualifier and stem to match the reasoning: "Which deployment handles the traffic pattern with the LEAST operational overhead?" (qualifier: "LEAST operational overhead"), or, if cost must remain the qualifier, add cost reasoning to each "why" and justify why pay-per-task Fargate beats Spot-backed EC2 capacity for this spiky pattern.

findings.message: The stem's Hint reproduces verbatim the first sentence of the explanation ("Zero-shot gives instructions with no examples; single-shot adds one worked example; multishot (few-shot) adds several."), which is precisely the first half of what the question asks ("When do zero-shot, single-shot and multishot prompting differ"). A learner who knows nothing can recite the definitional answer straight from the stem.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace the hint with a non-answering cue, e.g. "Hint: think about how many worked examples each technique supplies, and how many examples Anthropic recommends," or drop the hint entirely and narrow the stem to "How many examples should you add, and how should they be chosen and formatted?"

findings.message: Option A is the only option that carries a self-justifying clause restating the stem's requirement ("a new session starts from a copy of the history and the original is unchanged"), while B, C and D are bare option names; the length/detail asymmetry lets a learner pick the key by style rather than SDK knowledge.
findings.suggestedFix: Trim A to parallel phrasing, e.g. "Resume the session with fork_session=True.", and move the mechanism description into the explanation (which already states it).

findings.message: Option B's "why" asserts that any content placed after the tool_result blocks makes the request fail with a 400 naming the unresolved web_search tool use. The general Messages API permits additional text blocks in a user message after leading tool_result blocks, so this specific failure claim should be verified against current documentation; if trailing text does not actually break continuation, option B would also complete the turn and the card would have two workable answers.
findings.suggestedFix: Re-check the documented behavior for a user message that contains tool_result blocks plus trailing text while a server_tool_use is pending. If it does not 400, either reword option B so it clearly breaks the continuation (e.g. omits the tool_result or places text before it) or correct the "why" to state the real failure mode.

findings.message: Option b is word-for-word identical to keyed option a (only prefixed with "Adopt this approach:"), so two options state the same correct design and the learner cannot pick a single answer; option b's "why" also describes a VPC-CIDR-based database rule that its text no longer contains.
findings.suggestedFix: Restore the intended distractor for option b, e.g. "The load balancer group allows 443 from 0.0.0.0/0; the web group allows 80 and 443 only from the load balancer group; the database group allows 3306 from the VPC CIDR range." — which matches the existing "why".

findings.message: The explanation rebuts a VPC-range CIDR option ("CIDR-based rules, whether the VPC range or subnet ranges") that no option currently presents, leaving the rationale dangling.
findings.suggestedFix: After fixing option b to use the VPC CIDR, the explanation matches; otherwise drop the "whether the VPC range or" clause.

findings.message: The explanation rejects a DynamoDB option ("DynamoDB is the wrong data model for PL/SQL-heavy OLTP") that does not exist among the four options, so the answer text does not match the card and will confuse learners.
findings.suggestedFix: Delete the trailing DynamoDB clause from the explanation (or add a DynamoDB option to the MCQ if one was intended).

findings.message: The explanation states Lambda allocates CPU in proportion to memory "across 128 MB to 3,008 MB". The 3,008 MB ceiling was superseded in December 2020; Lambda functions can be configured up to 10,240 MB (10 GB), with proportional CPU up to ~6 vCPUs.
findings.suggestedFix: Change to: "Lambda allocates CPU in proportion to memory across 128 MB to 10,240 MB, with a full vCPU at 1,769 MB (and up to about 6 vCPUs at 10,240 MB) ..."

findings.message: Two numeric claims should be re-verified against current Files API documentation: the organization-wide storage total is given as 1 TB (Anthropic's documented figure has been 100 GB per organization), and an `expires_in_seconds` parameter with a 3,600–7,776,000 range is attributed to file uploads, which is not a documented Files API field in the versions I can confirm.
findings.suggestedFix: Re-check the total-storage figure and the existence/range of `expires_in_seconds` in the current Files API reference, and cite the doc page (add a `source`) so the numbers can be audited on future review dates.

findings.message: The stem's second half ("which Files API limits shape the fix") is under-determined relative to the answer: most limits listed (500 MB per file, the organization storage cap, expiry, download restrictions) have no bearing on the multi-tenant isolation fix — only the workspace cap (100 per organization) does — so a learner cannot know which limits are being asked for.
findings.suggestedFix: Narrow the stem, e.g. "What is wrong with that design, and what workspace/file-scoping limits constrain the fix?", or move the unrelated size/expiry/download limits into a clearly labelled "other limits worth knowing" aside in the explanation.

findings.message: The explanation states that ACM's managed renewal for DNS-validated certificates kicks in "45 days before expiry." ACM begins attempting automatic renewal of eligible (ACM-issued) certificates 60 days before expiration; 45 days is when ACM starts emitting daily "approaching expiration" notifications (which also apply to imported certificates), not when renewal is attempted.
findings.suggestedFix: Change to: "for DNS validation it begins attempting renewal 60 days before expiry, checking that the validation CNAME records still resolve in public DNS, then renews with no human action (ACM also emits daily expiration notifications starting 45 days out)."

findings.message: The keyed option is c (migrate to Aurora Global Database), but the stem's qualifier is "LEAST amount of change" and the explanation itself states the correct solution is the cross-Region read replica (option a), while option c's own "why" text says it "is the largest change on the list for a problem a read replica solves." The card is mis-keyed and teaches a false answer.
findings.suggestedFix: Set "correct": true on option a and "correct": false on option c; give option a a "why": null (or keyed-answer rationale) and keep option c's existing "why" as the distractor explanation.

findings.message: The stem's qualifier is "MOST highly available," but nothing in the options or the explanation concerns availability — the explanation and every "why" rank the options purely on cost per million tokens. On availability the options are indistinguishable (if anything, the Message Batches option in b is the least "available" since it is asynchronous), so the qualifier does not select the keyed answer.
findings.suggestedFix: Change the qualifier and stem to match the reasoning, e.g. qualifier "MOST cost-effective" and stem "Which change is the MOST cost-effective next step that preserves accuracy?"

findings.message: Option d references "Claude Fable 5.1" at $10 per million input tokens; this is not a recognizable Anthropic model name and appears to be a placeholder or typo, which undermines the card's credibility.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace with a real higher-tier model name and verify its current input price against the Anthropic pricing documentation.

findings.message: The stem's "Hint:" line is word-for-word the first clause of the explanation ("Tokens are the units a model actually reads and writes: words, subwords, characters or bytes"), so the first half of the two-part question ("What are tokens") is fully answered before the learner responds.
findings.suggestedFix: Drop the hint or replace it with a non-answering nudge, e.g. "Hint: think about what changes between model generations besides price per token."

findings.message: The closing sentence "Claude Opus 5, Sonnet 5 and Fable 5.1 have 200K-token windows; Haiku 4.5 has 200K" uses a contrastive semicolon but gives the identical figure on both sides, which signals a stale or mistyped number (and the model roster itself is tangential to a question about what the context window is). Re-verify each model's current window against the documentation.
findings.suggestedFix: Either collapse to a single clause (e.g. "Current Claude models — Opus 5, Sonnet 5, Fable 5.1 and Haiku 4.5 — expose 200K-token windows, with larger-window options available on some models") after confirming the figures, or drop the model-specific sentence entirely since the question asks only what the context window is and what counts toward it.

findings.message: Option d is a verbatim copy of keyed option a with only "Record the change in the team's runbook." appended, so it is equally correct; the learner cannot pick a single answer even though only a is keyed.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace option d with the Spot distractor its "why" describes, e.g. "Move the fleet to Spot Instances at the current m5.2xlarge size instead of buying a Savings Plan."

findings.message: The explanation rebuts distractors that no longer appear in the option list ("Spot reprices the wrong instance" and "consolidating onto larger instances"), and option d's "why" discusses Spot rather than the option's actual text, so the answer-side rationale does not match the card.
findings.suggestedFix: After fixing option d, align the explanation's rebuttals with the four options actually presented and remove the reference to a non-existent "consolidate onto larger instances" option.

findings.message: The stem ends with "Hint: the correct option begins \"Create a target tracking policy on a metric math expression ...\"", which literally identifies option A; a learner with no knowledge of SQS scaling can pick the key from that surface cue alone.
findings.suggestedFix: Delete the hint sentence from the question stem, ending it at "Which scaling configuration will process the backlog MOST effectively?"

findings.message: The key is the only option that echoes the stem's distinctive wording — the stem requires "stricter guardrails apply to production only" and option A is the only one containing "stricter ... policies to the production organizational unit" — and it is also the only option not opening with "Keep one account," so it stands out as the odd one on surface form alone. A learner who knows nothing about AWS account boundaries can pick it from these cues.
findings.suggestedFix: Reword the stem to avoid the shared keyword (e.g. "...that production-only guardrails can be enforced centrally") and normalize option openings so all four describe a boundary choice in parallel form (e.g. "Use separate subnets with distinct network ACLs in the existing account and VPC...", "Use a different Region for production within the existing account...").

findings.message: Option D's rationale says "the same ... SCP scope apply in both Regions," but the scenario is a single standalone account with no AWS Organizations mentioned, so SCPs would not be in play at all in that option; the reasoning is misleading as written.
findings.suggestedFix: Rewrite D's why as: "A Region separates infrastructure, not identities or billing: the same IAM principals govern both Regions, there is still no organizational boundary on which to attach production-only guardrails, and both Regions bill to the same account."

findings.message: Option C is a verbatim copy of the keyed option A (only prefixed with "Adopt this approach:") but is keyed incorrect, so two identically worded options are equally correct and the learner cannot pick a single answer. Option C's "why" text argues against a Multi-AZ design that its option text never describes, showing the intended Multi-AZ option body was lost.
findings.suggestedFix: Restore the intended distractor text for option C, e.g. "Run the dev/test database as a Multi-AZ RDS deployment and keep the Auto Scaling group running 24x7 on On-Demand instances so developers always have capacity.", which matches its existing "why" explanation.

findings.message: The explanation does not answer the stem at all: the question asks for Files API size/storage limits and self-expiration, but the explanation describes service accounts, federation issuers/rules, OIDC jwt-bearer token exchange and credential precedence. A learner is given an unrelated (and therefore wrong) answer, and no size limit, no total storage limit and no expiration mechanism are stated anywhere in the answer text.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace the explanation with the actual Files API answer, e.g.: per-file maximum upload size and total per-organization storage limit for the Files API, plus "set expires_in_seconds at upload time (or an expires_at) so the file is deleted automatically; 2592000 seconds = 30 days satisfies the compliance rule" — matching the curl snippet and realWorldUsage note.

findings.message: The card's central mechanism — an expires_in_seconds form field on POST /v1/files producing an expires_at on list results — is asserted only in the snippet and usage note and is not supported by any cited source; if the Files API does not accept that parameter, the card's whole premise fails.
findings.suggestedFix: Verify the expiration parameter name and the size/storage limit figures against the current Files API reference and add a source with a supporting quote.

findings.message: Option C's text is a verbatim duplicate of the keyed option A (only prefixed with "Proceed as follows:"), so two options describe the identical, correct Fargate-on-a-schedule solution and the learner cannot pick a single answer. C's "why" argues against a 24/7 patched host, which describes an EC2 solution that the option text does not actually state — evidence the option text was pasted in by mistake.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace option C's text with the EC2 solution its "why" describes, e.g. "Run the container on an Amazon EC2 instance in an Auto Scaling group, started once a day by a cron job on the instance."

findings.message: The stem's "Hint:" line is a verbatim copy of the first sentence of the explanation and literally states both request-format differences the question asks for (model in the URL path, and anthropic_version moved into the body with value vertex-2023-10-16), so a learner who knows nothing about Agent Platform can answer two-thirds of the card from the prompt alone.
findings.suggestedFix: Delete the Hint line, or replace it with a non-answering cue such as "Hint: think about what the SDK's AnthropicVertex(project_id=..., region=...) constructor has to rewrite before the call goes out."

findings.message: Both keyed options are pure word-matches to the stem's two stated requirements ('FedRAMP High' and 'AWS, not Anthropic, is the sole processor of inference data'), while all three distractors talk about unrelated topics (beta headers, Batches/Agent Skills, Marketplace billing). A learner with no knowledge of Bedrock can select a and c by surface term overlap alone.
findings.suggestedFix: Make the distractors plausible compliance/operator claims about Bedrock (e.g. 'Bedrock exempts customers from the AWS shared responsibility model', 'Bedrock routes inference through Anthropic's VPC under an AWS BAA', 'Bedrock inherits Anthropic's SOC 2 report in place of an AWS authorization') and paraphrase the keys so they do not repeat the stem's exact phrases (e.g. 'The service is operated by AWS, which acts as the processor for prompt and completion data' / 'It carries the government authorizations and DoD impact-level accreditations the contractor must evidence').

findings.message: Option b's 'why' asserts flatly that 'Bedrock does not accept the anthropic-beta header'; AWS documents passing an anthropic_beta field in the Anthropic request body on Bedrock for certain beta features, so this rationale is overstated even though the option's 'same-day feature parity' claim is wrong. Re-check this claim against current Bedrock documentation.
findings.suggestedFix: Reword the why to: 'Bedrock exposes only selected betas on the Bedrock release schedule, so new Claude API features do not arrive the same day; same-day beta access is a Claude Platform on AWS characteristic.'

findings.message: The stated qualifier (FEWEST model round trips) does not actually separate the key from option B: by option B's own "why", parallel calls also collapse the 20 lookups into a single assistant turn, so both A and B need one tool-issuing turn plus one final reporting turn. What uniquely decides for A is the second stem requirement (keeping raw line items out of the context window), not the round-trip count.
findings.suggestedFix: Re-anchor the qualifier on context, e.g. "Which change keeps the raw line items out of Claude's context window while using no more than one tool-issuing turn?", or adjust the explanation to say A ties B on round trips and wins on context isolation.

findings.message: Option (c) restates the keyed option (a) verbatim (only prefixed with "Adopt this approach:"), so two options describe the identical correct strategy and the learner cannot choose a single answer. Its "why" also argues against a nonexistent exception-handler approach, showing the option text was mis-pasted.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace option (c) with the approach its "why" actually rebuts, e.g. "Wrap the stream in a try/except for a RefusalError and log the exception when the stream ends early."

findings.message: Both the keyed option and the explanation rely on a field named "stop_details" accompanying a refusal stop_reason; this field name should be verified against current Anthropic streaming API documentation before publishing.
findings.suggestedFix: Confirm the exact response field that carries refusal detail (or drop the field name and say "show a user-facing message explaining the refusal").

findings.message: The explanation's phrase "retrying on a different Claude model with the fallback credit" appears garbled and does not correspond to anything in the stem or options.
findings.suggestedFix: Rewrite as "...or by retrying the request on a fallback model."

findings.message: The explanation does not answer the stem at all: the question asks how manual extended thinking is configured on Claude Haiku 4.5 and what rules budget_tokens follows, but the answer text discusses Files API uploads, workspace-scoped file_id visibility and per-tenant workspace isolation. A learner is given no correct answer to the question asked (and the stableUid 'ccdvf-extended-thinking-budget-tokens' confirms the explanation belongs to a different card).
findings.suggestedFix: Replace the explanation with the extended-thinking answer, e.g.: "Set thinking: {type: 'enabled', budget_tokens: N} on the Messages request. budget_tokens must be at least 1024 and must be less than max_tokens, since the thinking budget is drawn from the max_tokens allowance; it is a target for how many tokens Claude may spend reasoning, not a hard cap on total output. Larger budgets allow deeper reasoning but raise latency and cost, so pick the smallest budget that meets quality needs and leave headroom in max_tokens for the visible reply."

findings.message: The realWorldUsage cites usage.output_tokens_details.thinking_tokens as the field for inspecting thinking cost; this response field name cannot be confirmed against the Messages API usage object (thinking output is normally billed inside usage.output_tokens). The author should verify the exact field path against current documentation.
findings.suggestedFix: Re-check the usage field name in current API docs; if there is no separate thinking-token field, reword to "Compare usage.output_tokens with and without thinking enabled to see what a budget actually cost before raising it."

findings.message: The stem's "Hint:" line reproduces the first sentence of the explanation verbatim ("Create an origin group of a primary and a secondary origin and assign it to the cache behaviour"), so it hands the learner the entire "how do you make CloudFront fall back" half of the question before they answer.
findings.suggestedFix: Remove the hint, or replace it with a non-revealing nudge such as "Hint: think about how a single cache behaviour can reference two origins, and which HTTP methods qualify."

findings.message: The claim that unreachable-origin and timeout failover works "once 503 and 504 are listed" should be re-checked: CloudFront surfaces origin connection failures as 502 and origin timeouts as 504, so 503 looks like the wrong code to cite here.
findings.suggestedFix: Verify against the current CloudFront origin failover documentation and state the codes precisely, e.g. "...or cannot be reached or times out, provided 502 and 504 are among the configured failover status codes."

findings.message: The explanation ends with "Macie finds sensitive data; it never authorizes access," but no option mentions Amazon Macie — this looks like leftover text from a different card's option set and will confuse learners reviewing the answer.
findings.suggestedFix: Delete the Macie sentence, or replace one distractor (e.g. option c) with an Amazon Macie-based option so the explanation matches the options.

findings.message: The keying is inverted: option b (aws:SourceIp) is marked "correct": true, yet its own "why" text explains why it fails (it still permits direct kms:Decrypt from office IPs and would block S3's requests), and the explanation states the answer is the kms:ViaService + kms:CallerAccount condition — which is option a, currently keyed false with a null "why".
findings.suggestedFix: Set option a ("kms:ViaService equal to s3.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com and kms:CallerAccount equal to the account ID") to "correct": true with "why": null, and set option b to "correct": false, keeping its existing "why" text as the rationale for why the source-IP condition is wrong.

findings.message: The keyed answer is option d ("Parse the text anyway and ship it"), but the card's own explanation and d's "why" text say consuming a truncated report as complete is the failure mode; the genuinely correct first action is option a (treat as truncated, don't parse, enable compaction/context editing). The correct flags are swapped.
findings.suggestedFix: Set "correct": true on option a (and give it why: null as the keyed answer) and "correct": false on option d, keeping d's existing "why" as the rejection rationale.

findings.message: The stem's qualifier is "MOST cost-effective", but nothing in the card ranks options by cost: the explanation and every "why" argue enforceability (prompts are advisory, the callback is bypassed, unlisted tools still run). By the stated cost qualifier, option b (one line in the system prompt) is the cheapest to implement, so the qualifier does not select the keyed hook answer — the real deciding criterion is reliability of enforcement.
findings.suggestedFix: Change the qualifier to match the reasoning, e.g. stem: "Which implementation MOST reliably enforces this requirement?" with mcq.qualifier set to "MOST reliably enforces the requirement".

findings.message: The stem's only stated requirements are that sessions survive instance loss/scale-in and that sticky sessions are not used, plus the vague phrase "an acceptable option"; options C (RDS MySQL Multi-AZ) and D (EFS) both also satisfy those requirements, and their "why" texts reject them on latency and throughput — a criterion the stem never states. The deciding criterion (low per-request lookup latency) is missing from the stem.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace "and it wants an acceptable option" with an explicit deciding criterion, e.g. "...without enabling sticky sessions, and session lookups must complete with sub-millisecond latency on every request. Which solution meets these requirements?" (or add a qualifier such as "Which solution provides the LOWEST session-lookup latency?").

findings.message: Option B is explicitly excluded by the stem ("without enabling sticky sessions"), and its own "why" admits "the question also rules it out", so no learner would select it; it adds no discriminating value.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace B with a plausible shared-session distractor that is not pre-excluded, e.g. "Store sessions in Amazon DynamoDB with a TTL attribute" is already used in the explanation — or use "Write sessions to an Amazon S3 bucket keyed by session ID" — and explain why it is inferior on the stated latency criterion.

findings.message: The "why" for option B asserts that "the documented remedy is a prompt for a fixed cadence (one consult before substantive work, one before finishing)", which conflicts with the explanation's flat statement that "A prompt plea does not restore that detection" and points learners to a remedy that no option offers and that the keyed answer does not use.
findings.suggestedFix: Rewrite B's "why" to stay within the card's logic, e.g.: "A consult instruction keyed to the executor's own judgment cannot help when low effort is exactly what stopped it from noticing it is stuck; it leaves both the consult rate and the effort setting unchanged."

findings.message: Internal inconsistency on capacity: the stem says the existing Site-to-Site VPN is saturating, and option b's "why" puts a standard tunnel's cap at 1.25 Gbps, yet the explanation computes the flow at only ~300 Mbps and argues a 1 Gbps port "leaves headroom". If 100 TB/month truly saturates a 1.25 Gbps tunnel, a 1 Gbps hosted connection would not have headroom.
findings.suggestedFix: Reconcile the numbers, e.g. state in the stem that the replication window is compressed into a few hours each night (so peaks exceed the VPN tunnel limit even though the monthly average is ~300 Mbps), or drop the "saturating" premise and justify Direct Connect purely on the private-path and egress-cost requirements.

findings.message: The explanation asserts that "a Read deny also blocks Edit and Write on the same path," which would make the separate "Edit(./.env*)" entry in the keyed option redundant — the card contradicts itself on whether the Edit deny rule is needed. This cross-tool inheritance claim should be verified against current Claude Code permission documentation.
findings.suggestedFix: Either drop the cross-tool claim (e.g. "deny rules are evaluated before ask and allow in every permission mode, so both the Read and Edit patterns are needed to cover reading and rewriting") or, if Read deny genuinely covers Edit/Write, state that the Edit rule is belt-and-braces.

findings.message: The realWorldUsage note states that an alarm on UnHealthyHostCount with the Minimum statistic greater than 0 is "the AWS-recommended early warning". AWS documentation recommends the Maximum statistic for UnHealthyHostCount (and Minimum for HealthyHostCount); Minimum > 0 only fires when every load balancer node reports an unhealthy target, which is a later, not earlier, signal than the keyed HealthyHostCount alarm.
findings.suggestedFix: Change to: "Add a companion alarm on UnHealthyHostCount Maximum greater than 0 for more than one data point; AWS recommends the Maximum statistic for UnHealthyHostCount, giving an early warning before the healthy count falls."

findings.message: The stem explicitly asks for the role of `${VAR:-default}`, but the explanation only states that `${VAR}` and `${VAR:-default}` "expand" in .mcp.json without ever saying that the `:-default` form supplies a fallback value when the variable is unset or empty — so the question's second sub-part is not actually answered.
findings.suggestedFix: Add to the explanation: "`${VAR}` substitutes the environment variable and fails if it is unset; `${VAR:-default}` substitutes the variable when set and otherwise falls back to `default` (e.g. `"url": "${MCP_URL:-http://localhost:3000/mcp}"`)."

findings.message: The explanation rebuts an option that does not exist on the card ("Shield Advanced answers volumetric DDoS, not a single noisy address"); no option mentions Shield Advanced, which will confuse learners reviewing the answer.
findings.suggestedFix: Delete the Shield Advanced sentence from the explanation, or add a Shield Advanced distractor option so the rebuttal matches an actual choice.

findings.message: The explanation states a Kinesis data stream retains records "24 hours by default and up to 7 days". Since long-term retention was introduced, the maximum retention for a data stream is 365 days (7 days is only the limit of extended retention at the standard extended-retention price), so the stated ceiling is no longer true.
findings.suggestedFix: Reword to: "A data stream keeps records for 24 hours by default, up to 7 days with extended retention and up to 365 days with long-term retention, so 7-day replay is just a retention setting."

findings.message: The long-context statement is wrong on two counts: Anthropic's >200K long-context pricing is not applied only to the tokens "beyond 200K" — once a request's prompt exceeds the 200K threshold, the premium rate applies to the whole request's input tokens, and output tokens are also billed at a premium long-context rate, not just input.
findings.suggestedFix: Rewrite as: "For requests whose prompt exceeds 200K tokens in the 1M context window, all input tokens and all output tokens of that request are billed at the long-context premium rates (not just the tokens above 200K)."

findings.message: The stem asks which modifiers stack, but the answer never says how the long-context premium interacts with the Batch discount or cache multipliers, leaving part of the question unanswered for the one modifier it introduces last.
findings.suggestedFix: Add a clause stating whether the long-context premium combines with batch (50%) and cache multipliers, e.g. "the long-context premium applies to the base rate first, and batch/cache modifiers then apply on top."

findings.message: Two specific figures cannot be confirmed against documentation and should be re-verified before publishing: the 0.025x cache-hit rate attributed to "Claude Fable 5.1" (all other models are stated at 0.1x) and the 1.1x inference_geo "us" multiplier applying to every token category for 4.6-and-later models.
findings.suggestedFix: Re-check the 0.025x cache-hit rate and the 1.1x inference_geo multiplier against the current Anthropic pricing page, and cite the page in source.

findings.message: The stem explicitly diagnoses the cause ("two image blocks with no labels"), and only the keyed option mentions labeling ("each preceded by a short label such as \"Image 1:\""); options b, c and d never mention labels, so a learner with no knowledge of Claude's image-ordering guidance can match the stem's "no labels" wording to the key.
findings.suggestedFix: State only the symptom in the stem, e.g. "...sends the question as the first content block, followed by two image blocks. Answers often refer to the wrong screenshot." — drop "with no labels" so the labeling fix is not pre-announced.

findings.message: The stem's "Hint:" is the verbatim first sentence of the explanation, so it already states the answer to the first half of the question (declare the dependency as an object with name plus a semver range instead of a bare string). A learner who knows nothing about plugin dependencies gets the answer from the prompt side before answering.
findings.suggestedFix: Delete the hint, or replace it with a non-answering nudge such as "Hint: think about how the dependency entry can express an acceptable version window, and what Claude Code matches that window against in the dependency's repository."

findings.message: The explanation does not answer the stem at all: the question asks why Trusted Advisor's idle-EC2 and underused-EBS checks are missing on the Basic support plan and what Trusted Advisor covers, but the explanation text is entirely about CloudFront versus AWS Global Accelerator (static anycast IPs, UDP listeners, traffic dials). A learner is given a wrong answer for this card's question.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace the explanation with Trusted Advisor content, e.g.: "Cost-optimisation checks such as Low Utilization Amazon EC2 Instances and Underutilized Amazon EBS Volumes require a Business, Enterprise On-Ramp or Enterprise Support plan. Basic and Developer plans receive only the core set: all service quota checks plus a handful of security checks (e.g. public S3 buckets, security group ports unrestricted, MFA on root account, IAM use, EBS/RDS public snapshots). Trusted Advisor spans five pillars — cost optimisation, performance, security, fault tolerance and service limits — but only the full check set unlocks with paid support."

findings.message: Option C repeats option B's text verbatim ("permissions.deny rule ... in managed settings deployed to every machine") and only adds a runbook note, so it satisfies the "MOST reliable" qualifier exactly as well as the keyed option B; a learner cannot pick a single answer. Its "why" also argues against *user* settings, which its own text does not describe, confirming the option text is wrong.
findings.suggestedFix: Rewrite option C to match its rationale, e.g. "Ask each engineer to add the permissions.deny rule for infra/prod/ to their own user settings (~/.claude/settings.json)."

findings.message: The stated per-batch cap of "10,000 requests or 32 MB" was the original Message Batches limit at launch; current documentation puts a batch at up to 100,000 requests or 256 MB, whichever is reached first. The scenario's conclusion (150,000 requests / 300 MB must be split) still holds, but the quoted numbers would teach a learner the wrong caps.
findings.suggestedFix: Change to: "A single batch holds at most 100,000 requests or 256 MB, whichever is hit first, so this 150,000-request / 300 MB job must be split; oversized payloads fail with 413 request_too_large."

findings.message: The specific Claude Opus 5 batch prices ($2.50 per million input / $12.50 per million output, implying $5/$25 standard) are asserted without a source and cannot be confirmed; if they are wrong the card teaches incorrect pricing.
findings.suggestedFix: Re-check Opus 5 input/output pricing against the current pricing page, or drop the dollar figures and keep only the model-agnostic rule that batch pricing is 50% of standard input, output and special-token rates.

findings.message: The stem asks which grading method fits each of three criteria, but the explanation only explicitly maps two (categorical → code-based, tone → LLM-based); the "no leaked personal data" criterion is never assigned a method, so the learner cannot self-check the third part of the answer.
findings.suggestedFix: Add an explicit mapping for the third criterion, e.g. "No leaked personal data: code-based grading — regex/string match for PII patterns (emails, phone numbers, card and account numbers) against the known customer record, since a deterministic check is faster and more reliable than a judge for a pattern-matchable criterion."

findings.message: The stem only asks which option is "an acceptable way to run this workload" and states no cost, overhead, or other deciding criterion, yet every distractor is rejected purely on cost/idle waste (an EC2 instance, a Fargate service, or a Spot Instance would all functionally run 2,000 three-second resizes a day). Without a qualifier, four options satisfy the stem as written and a careful learner cannot pick one.
findings.suggestedFix: Add the deciding qualifier to the stem, e.g. "Which compute option is the MOST cost-effective way to run this workload?", and set mcq.qualifier to "MOST cost-effective".

findings.message: The explanation is about the pilot light disaster-recovery strategy (RDS replicas, Auto Scaling at zero capacity, RPO/RTO) and never addresses the stem's question about IAM permissions boundaries, so the answer text is wrong for this card; it also contradicts the card's own topic (1.1 Secure access), codeSnippet (an iam:PermissionsBoundary condition) and realWorldUsage note.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace the explanation with the permissions-boundary answer, e.g.: "A permissions boundary is a managed policy attached to the developer's principal that caps the maximum permissions of any role it creates: grant iam:CreateRole/iam:AttachRolePolicy only with a Condition on iam:PermissionsBoundary so every role the developer creates must carry the DevBoundary policy, and the role's effective permissions are the intersection of its identity policy and the boundary. A restrictive identity policy on the developers only limits what the developers themselves can do — it does not restrict the permissions policies they can attach to a new role, so without the boundary condition they could create a role with Administrator access and assume or pass it (privilege escalation)."

findings.message: The explanation's closing sentence says "Batch size 1, a longer visibility timeout and a DLQ each leave the good messages retried," but batch size 1 does not leave good messages retried — each message is its own batch, so only the malformed one is redelivered. This also contradicts option a's own "why", which states "It does stop the nine good messages from being retried."
findings.suggestedFix: Rewrite as: "A longer visibility timeout and a DLQ each still leave the good messages retried; batch size 1 does stop the duplicates but destroys batching throughput, so it is not the most efficient fix."

findings.message: The explanation's rundown of wrong options includes "more Lambda memory changes nothing," but no option proposes increasing Lambda memory; the four options are usage plans, reserved concurrency, WAF rate-based rule, and an SQS buffer. The stray clause suggests the explanation was written for a different option set and may confuse learners.
findings.suggestedFix: Delete "and more Lambda memory changes nothing" from the explanation (or add a memory-sizing distractor if one was intended).

findings.message: Option C states exactly the same design as the keyed option A ("Define three subagents and let them run concurrently so the review finishes in the time of the slowest check") plus an irrelevant runbook note, so it is equally correct and a learner cannot choose a single answer.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace option C's text with the distinct distractor its "why" describes, e.g. "Use a single subagent with a large context window to run all three checks."

findings.message: Option C's "why" ("One subagent still performs the checks one after another; window size does not create parallelism") does not explain the option as written, which describes three concurrent subagents and a runbook entry.
findings.suggestedFix: Align the "why" with the corrected option text, or if C keeps concurrent subagents, explain that recording the change in a runbook does not affect latency.

findings.message: The stem only asks which change is "acceptable" and states no qualifier, but option B (adding a single example of the desired line) is also an acceptable, on-technique change — its own "why" concedes it is "the right technique at the wrong dose," i.e. it works, just less reliably. Without a "MOST reliable/effective" criterion a careful learner cannot choose between A and B.
findings.suggestedFix: Rewrite the stem with an explicit qualifier, e.g. "Which prompt change is MOST likely to produce a consistent one-line \"category: reason\" output?" (and set mcq.qualifier accordingly), so the 3-to-5-example dose is the deciding factor.

findings.message: The keying is inverted: option b (attach an IAM policy to the root user) is marked correct even though its own "why" text and the explanation both state that IAM identity policies do not limit the root user, so the restriction has no effect. Option a (enable MFA, delete root access keys, move the script to a least-privilege IAM role) is the answer the explanation actually describes but it is keyed false.
findings.suggestedFix: Set option a "correct": true (and leave its "why" null), and set option b "correct": false, keeping its existing "why" as the rejection rationale.

findings.message: The explanation and option b's "why" both state that a Lambda invocation is capped at 300 seconds (5 minutes). AWS Lambda's maximum function timeout has been 900 seconds (15 minutes) since 2018, and the card's own explanation contradicts itself by later saying "event-driven work under 15 minutes is Lambda."
findings.suggestedFix: Change both the explanation and option b's "why" to state the Lambda maximum timeout is 900 seconds (15 minutes), which is still far short of a 2–6 hour job.

findings.message: The explanation states Lambda's payload ceilings are "6 MB synchronous or 1 MB asynchronous." The synchronous (RequestResponse) limit is 6 MB, but the asynchronous (Event) invocation payload limit is 256 KB, not 1 MB.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace "a 6 MB synchronous or 1 MB asynchronous payload" with "a 6 MB synchronous or 256 KB asynchronous invocation payload".

findings.message: Option b's "why" asserts that "Lambda Managed Instances, which run on EC2 capacity you pay for, stretch asynchronous runs to 90 minutes." This specific product name and 90-minute figure should be verified against current Lambda documentation, since it is the only justification offered for the extended-duration claim.
findings.suggestedFix: Re-check the Lambda Managed Instances name and maximum asynchronous run duration against current AWS Lambda documentation, or drop that clause and rely solely on the 15-minute standard ceiling to rule out option b.

findings.message: Option c is a verbatim duplicate of the keyed option a (only prefixed with "Proceed as follows:"), so two options are equally correct and the learner cannot pick the single keyed answer. Option c's "why" text (about temperature/determinism) and the explanation's mention of temperature show the intended distractor text was lost.
findings.suggestedFix: Restore the intended distractor for option c, e.g. "Set temperature to 0 so the model's output is deterministic.", which matches its existing "why" and the explanation's reference to temperature.

findings.message: The explanation (and the realWorldUsage note) devotes most of its length to a secondary-ENI / hot-standby-in-same-AZ scenario and to rules about primary interfaces and AZ boundaries that no option in this card involves, which obscures why option A is keyed.
findings.suggestedFix: Trim the explanation to the Elastic IP reasoning and the rejection of B/C/D (e.g., drop the sentence beginning "An Elastic IP moves only the public address..."), and change the realWorldUsage note to reference only the Elastic IP reassociation automation rather than "script the interface attach".

findings.message: The stem explicitly includes an on-premises InfluxDB, but the answer only mentions "open-source and third-party sources" generically and never explains how Managed Grafana reaches a private on-prem source (network connectivity to the customer VPC/on-prem network via the workspace's privately connected data source / VPC configuration). The learner is left without the part of the answer the stem specifically set up.
findings.suggestedFix: Add a sentence such as: "For the on-premises InfluxDB, use the Grafana InfluxDB data source plugin and attach the workspace to a VPC (network access control / VPC connectivity) that reaches on premises over Direct Connect or Site-to-Site VPN."

findings.message: The distractor "why" texts are prefixed with internal authoring-taxonomy labels ("Real technical error variable:", "Mechanism for the wrong scope:", "Over-engineering:") that are editorial notes rather than learner-facing explanation, and they appear in the text shown after answering.
findings.suggestedFix: Strip the classification prefixes, e.g. b: "max_uses only limits how many fetches run; the URL is rejected before any fetch is counted, so retries fail identically." c: "allowed_domains filters which hosts may be fetched and yields url_not_allowed; url_not_in_prior_context means the URL's source is disallowed regardless of domain." d: "A search may surface a different page, and the URL is already known — it only needs to appear in an allowed place."

findings.message: The claim that Claude Code "adds it to your global git excludes" is doubtful: the documented behavior is that the local settings file is excluded at the repository level (project .gitignore / .git/info/exclude), not in the user's global excludes file. This detail should be re-checked against current documentation.
findings.suggestedFix: Change to "...Claude Code writes standing approvals there and keeps it out of version control (it is excluded for the repository, e.g. via .gitignore), so it is never committed."

findings.message: The explanation states "an object can reach 50 TB". The maximum S3 object size is 5 TB (50 TB is just the arithmetic product of 10,000 parts x 5 GB, which is not the enforced object-size limit).
findings.suggestedFix: Change to "an object can reach 5 TB" (10,000 parts of up to 5 GB, capped at the 5 TB maximum object size).

findings.message: The per-prefix request rates cited ("at least 100 PUT, COPY, POST or DELETE and 300 GET or HEAD requests per second per partitioned prefix") are the pre-2018 figures; since July 2018 S3 supports at least 3,500 PUT/COPY/POST/DELETE and 5,500 GET/HEAD requests per second per partitioned prefix.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace with "at least 3,500 PUT, COPY, POST or DELETE and 5,500 GET or HEAD requests per second per partitioned prefix".
